utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I believe you said you had one more matter to raise with the witness, or are you finished?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't get any interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to put another question to this witness, and that will be my final question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Are you getting interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Ivasov, yesterday we started discussing the meeting which you attended together with Chernomyrdin, Atasari, and the entire Russian delegation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the time, we were guaranteed a sovereignty, territorial integrity, and then the issue discussed was the arrival of the UN security forces which was to guarantee the security of all citizens living in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that, in view of the fact that our country was not defeated in that war, we raised an issue with your entire delegation, headed by Chernomyrdin, to the effect that we could not agree to these forces being introduced pursuant to Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which specifies that the forces used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's all leading questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't think it's relevant. Move on -- if that's the only question, then your examination-in-chief is at an end. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to put my question. I need to put my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you must put it in a way which is not leading and which makes it relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very relevant, very relevant indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General Ivasov, is it true that Chernomyrdin, in his capacity of envoy of President Yeltsin and as representative of Russia guaranteed to us on behalf of Russia and President Yeltsin that their resolution would not be passed pursuant to Chapter VII and that should there be any attempts to pass it based on Chapter VII, Russia would veto it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's an entirely leading question. The time must arise --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite apart from its leading nature, I rule it to be irrelevant. So that concludes the examination-in-chief, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have ruled on it. Mr. Nice, begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you are not being heard. Your examination-in-chief is at an end. Mr. Nice will begin his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Ivasov, you made a number of general, broad assertions yesterday which may be interpreted as allegations against the United States of America, NATO, I think even the United Kingdom. I want you to understand that I have absolutely no interest in defending the United States or NATO or the United Kingdom, and that if these allegations of yours are relevant to this trial, and if they may be shown to be true, it's far better that they emerge in this trial. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to understand that it's no part of my function to attack your evidence as unreliable or as untrue. It's my duty simply to test it, and that is what I will do. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that there can be no mistake about this in light of many of the questions asked of you by the accused, you, General Ivasov, coming, of course, from what was for a long time a communist country, will understand that the standards to be applied in testing your evidence will be the same as the standards that will be applied in testing the evidence of an ordinary Kosovo Albanian villager, and you would expect no different, would you? You would expect no different, would you, General?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I protest against my country being accused of having lived in the socialist period and your reproach or hint that I will fail to be objective because of that. It's not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You observed yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. I certainly didn't understand that as a reproach. I understood that to be emphasising the principle of communism that everyone was treated equally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the dispute between capitalism and communism is not subject for discussion in this audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, General, that - at page 12 of the transcript the way I have it paginated - that you relied on -- no. Let me go right back to the beginning in case there are any people who didn't -- who currently is viewing the proceedings who didn't see it yesterday. Your clear thesis is that the United States of America had and pursued a preconceived plan to destroy the former Yugoslavia. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us yesterday, page 12, that you relied on various types of information and analyses. Did you receive analyses in completed form from subordinates and act on that, or did you conduct the analysis of raw material yourself?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted this analysis both myself, by obtaining vast information, information which testified to the fact that starting from 1998, January of 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... detail will come later. You conducted the analysis yourself --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted the analysis myself, and the analysis was also conducted by rather strong departments of the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Chief of Staff, and the special services, and this conclusion was a common conclusion of those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... General, not substance. Now, from what you've told us, then, you should be in a position to explain exactly what raw material there was to work upon. Correct or not?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question was a simple one. Are you able to tell us what was the raw material relied upon for this conclusion about the plan of the United States of America? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your answer that there was, as it were, an intervening intermediate level of reporting by those who conducted analyses on your behalf. Let's just have an answer to this straight away: Are those written analyses available for this Court to read; and will they be provided by you or by Russia?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can be provided by Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why haven't you brought them with you?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought with me all the -- those things which today are not classified. Yesterday I showed to you a declassified analysis of the General Staff of the Russian Federation. Here it is. I'm holding it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's pursue that. From your answer, there was clearly some reporting or analysis that is classified. Are you going to be able to produce that to us or not?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can present only those things which are declassified today and published, and I will present such things if need be. Those things which today are still a secret, I have no authority to discuss this. And moreover, the United States or NATO never presented such documents themselves. Today I can present only expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are not concerned at the moment with what America does. And this Chamber is aware, because it has to deal with the processes for compelling production of documents by states, of the privileges that some countries hold, but you have chosen to come here and make extraordinarily broad allegations and you're now telling us, are you, that some of this is on the basis of secret information that you won't tell us about. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready to present part of those documents and of those analyses of the General Staff which have been declassified, and I'm convinced that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those documents would be sufficient for tendering in court. Those documents which are a secret are beyond my authority to -- for me to tender them here and present them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, you will understand that it's not your judgement on what is sufficient in this court that counts. The three gentlemen whose judgement matters are sitting in front of me. You have chosen, without it being absolutely plain, to give opinions based on material that you're now -- or material that you're going to keep secret. Let's explore that material, shall we?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm saying that this is my opinion, and this is what I think. However, I'm not the one to judge whether that material will be sufficient or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just take an example, General, before we return to the substance of your evidence. If you were to, in your capacity as a military leader, to advise your political masters that they should attack some other country, and if your political masters wanted to see the raw material justifying your decision, would you say that it would be appropriate for them to see that material, or would you say that you would be entitled to keep it from them?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my authorities, I report that information which I receive from different sources, as well as the minutes of my meetings with Mr. Hun [phoen], with Mr. Robinson, with Mr. Slocum, Warner, Naumann, Solana, and others. And on the basis of those negotiations and different documents, on the basis of the participation in various conferences, my subordinates and myself, we analyse that material and report to our authorities. And when the authorities receive from various sources - not only my sources but other sources as well - various materials, conclusions and data, the authorities have the capability to draw its own conclusions and form and shape its own position, and this is a classical scheme of work of any military institution. If you would like to ask me for any specifics, I can quote here specific examples or quotes from my meetings with the Secretary-General of NATO and also ministers of defence of NATO Member States and also deputy ministers of the United States, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, that is a long answer, not responsive to a simple question. If you were advising your political masters to take some grave action and they asked to see the raw material, would you show it to them?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I showed to my superiors such materials, but my materials were not the only sources for drawing conclusions and decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's examine the material that you declined to make available to this Court. In forming your opinion, did you have intercept of telephone conversations of, let us say, Presidents Bush and Clinton to work on? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the first observation, I'm not refusing to tender any documents in court. I'm only stating that I'm able to tender only such materials which have been published and which are declassified. Secondly, I believe that this is not subject to debate whether we ever listened to intercepts or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- speeches or conversations from Clinton and Yeltsin, et cetera. This is a different level of confidentiality. I refuse to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hadn't asked you, but it's helpful to know that you should assume I was inquiring into the army's -- please listen to me. That you should assume I was inquiring into the army's intercepting its own president for it was not a question that I asked in those terms at all. We will draw our own inferences from that. It is not for you to decide what is relevant. It is for the Judges. The question is, please: In forming your extraordinarily strong conclusion, General Ivasov, did you have intercepts of telephone conversations of Western leaders? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can affirm only one thing, that the telephones of Hashim Thaci were bugged by the Serbian services, and the Russian side participated. But those were the telephone conversations between -- with the head of a terrorist organisation. That was quite legal. And I can confirm that Ms. Albright also participated in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That in the fact that she -- I can actually give you -- quote two examples: September 1998, when Ms. Albright advised Hashim Thaci to agree to the introduction of NATO troops to Kosovo, and in response she would guarantee the conduct of a referendum for Kosovo's independence. On the 25th of April, 1999, on the second day after the commencement of the bombardment of Yugoslavia, Ms. Albright demanded that the KLA would raise an insurgency, and in response in Rambouillet, Mr. Hashim Thaci made a statement, and I can quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go on. Document with you --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to outline the efforts of the American Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. In the press communique which was made by Hashim Thaci, he outlines: "I would like to especially outline the tireless efforts of the American Secretary of State Albright," and further on, "Kosovo invites the NATO forces and expects their soon deployment." So here I'm talking about the connections between the terrorists and the officials of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General. General, what document did you just read from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This -- these documents are the documents of the Yugoslav army's services. These are not documents, these are radio and telephone intercepts of Hashim Thaci, the head of terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you make them available to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is the internal matter of the current government of the Republic of Serbia and Montenegro. I cannot do this on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, if you start reading from documents in court, prima facie the Court is entitled to see it and probably take possession of it. Can you make it available to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm responding to your question, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think he was saying he wouldn't make it available. Pass it over to the usher. Yes, the document that you just read from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say that I have no authority to provide this document because I have no power to do so. I did not receive any mandate to do so, either from my government or the government of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will realise, then, Mr. Milosevic, that the evidence is almost valueless. If the document that he read come cannot be passed over to the Court for the reasons that he just outlined, the evidence is valueless, because it is not, then, going to be able to be tested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to protest very emphatically. Mr. Nice is badgering this witness, a very renowned witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. There is no badgering of the witness. He's perfectly entitled to put every single question that he has to the witness, and you should have organised your examination of this witness in such a way that the witness would be able to substantiate what he said in court with documents which are available. The evidence is totally meaningless if it cannot be tested, if he's not in a position to pass over to the Court the document that he just read from. I'll consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you might want to ascertain during the break whether the general can receive the authority that he says is necessary to hand over the document. Until that is done, speaking for myself, I would not attach much weight to the evidence that he has given because the Court is not in a position to see the document. We don't even know whether what he has read is actually in the document or what else is in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already asked you, Mr. Robinson, whether you doubt that General Ivasov, who enjoys great repute both in the East and the West is speaking the truth or not. He is at the top of the military pyramid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. It's not for you to ask me any questions. We will determine what weight to attach to the evidence, and I've told you that this evidence, as far as I'm concerned, is practically worthless if the Prosecutor and the Court is not able to see the document from which he just read. If you want us to attach -- if you want me to attach any weight to it, you must get the authority from Russia which is needed for him to hand it over to the Court so that we can look at it. From Serbia, rather, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General -- go ahead. Is the document what you read a minute ago an intercept or original report or a summary made by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement of Hashim Thaci that I just read out was published in open press. The two excerpts that I read earlier were indeed intercepts, intercepts made by secret services. After this hearing, I can leave in this court these documents of the General Staff, and I underline that these are documents and a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. monograph of the General Staff written based on many, many documents, declassified documents related to the Kosovo crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I would not allow the witness to read out a document which cannot be passed on to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will take this into account. But there is certain information that I received in the course of my discussions with the high officials of various countries. How are we to treat that information? For instance, my discussions with Deputy Defence Ministers Slocum and Warner, who were the first to show me that, from the beginning of 1998, a course was taken to force Yugoslavia to accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The issues that you just raised go fundamentally to how the accused manages his case. He's mismanaging the case, because you are seeking to introduce evidence here to make allegations which require for their substantiation certain documents, and you do not have the documents. In those circumstances, the Chamber, in my view, will not be in a position to attach much weight to the evidence. Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would like to deal with what I think is a basic misunderstanding on your part of our position. I certainly would never reach a final judgement on the credibility or reliability of any witness at all in this case until I'd heard all the evidence in the case, and therefore it's important, when you lead evidence from any witness, to do all that you possibly can to reinforce the credibility and reliability of that witness. That's number one. The second point is a point of clarification. I wish to ask the general a question, which may be a problem of translation or interpretation. You indicated that the Serbian authorities did bug Thaci with assistance from Russia, and you then said that Albright also participated. Did you mean to say that, as a result of doing so, you were intercepting her conversation, or did you mean to say that the United States were involved in that exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just saying, for the record, that Madam Albright speak to Mr. Thaci, Hashim Thaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me clarify what I said earlier. Mr. Milosevic, as an accused, there is absolutely no burden on you to prove anything. You can sit there and remain totally silent, absolutely silent. The legal burden is on the Prosecutor to prove the allegations in the indictment. But to the extent that you adduce evidence, and you wish - don't speak when I'm speaking - and you wish the Court to take account of that evidence, then you must do so in a manner which makes the evidence as credible as possible, otherwise the Chamber will not be in a position to attach much weight to it, and this is the position we find ourselves in at this stage. Mr. Nice, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, just let us make one thing clear. I would like us to understand each other. Far be it from me to think that you are disputing the credibility of General Ivasov. That's one. And second, on the basis of what do you assume that the entire book of documents which have been declassified and then published does not contain anything of any use to you? General Ivasov told you the documents that have been declassified, from which the stamp "Official Secret" has been removed, were included in the book. Look in these documents and you will see. And generally speaking, the minutes and his evidence on his discussions with the officials of the NATO alliance concerning the attack on Yugoslavia is a major issue. I don't see how anyone can dispute that these discussions took place and that in the course of these discussions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are now discussing the particular document from which the witness just read and which he's not in a position to hand over to the Court. A novel position for me. Mr. Nice, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I ask my next question, can I, just for convenience, summarise the position. The document that the accused just referred to, which is, I think, the red-coloured book that the witness has held up, was not served in advance, has not been translated, was not relied on in any substantive way if at all in evidence-in-chief, and it is simply not realistic or acceptable to ask us post the evidence of the witness to conduct our own analysis in a way that may be favourable to the accused. Procedurally, the accused has to understand, and I'm sure the Court -- well, the Court's been making this point to him, that if he wants to rely on a document, it has to be prepared in advance, served in advance if it's a substantial document for me to deal with. I am anxious not to waste the Court's time with having this witness's evidence adjourned, but if the accused actually wants us to consider that book, then out of his budget of time, he would have to ask now for arrangements to be made for the book to be translated, to reopen his examination-in-chief, and to take the witness through the relevant parts of it. I don't ask for that to happen, and I hope it won't, but that is what he should be doing. Second, the general has so for declined and refused to answer questions about intercepts generally. He's made one selection that he obviously came prepared with, and he's refused to hand the piece of paper over. I will carry on asking him questions, but depending on his response, the time may come when I shall ask that his evidence be disregarded altogether. The solemn declaration that witnesses take is to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. That obliges them not to be selective. And if they become selective, the question of their attitude toward the Court is at large, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it is clear to you that the testimony of General Ivasov about the fact that the Clinton administration had planned the aggression on Yugoslavia is not based on one single detail that he mentioned in passing, this intercept of a conversation between Hashim Thaci and Mrs. Albright. There are many other facts in which this is grounded, and among those facts are his own personal conversations with NATO officials. So even if you choose to completely discount this intercept, you can take his evidence that it was so and these issues were raised at the highest level within the framework of the cooperation between Russia and NATO. That fact is indisputable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, you told us you're not going to answer the question about intercepts as between Western leaders, remembering that you also answered about intercepting your own political leaders. You then selected one intercept that you have noted about Mrs. Albright. Let's go back to the original question. Are you going to change your answer about --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say one thing. We were listening, eavesdropping on Hashim Thaci, a terrorist. We were not listening to the conversations of Mrs. Albright. This is essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question is are you now prepared to tell us - yes or no - because we're at the stage of methodology --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice insinuated to General Ivasov that we were listening to their own military -- sorry, political leaders, whereas General Ivasov never said anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think General Ivasov just clarified what he was listening to. Continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you now prepared to tell us - yes or no - whether your raw material included intercepts of conversations between Western leaders? Yes or no, General.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about intercepts of conversations between Western leaders are not available to me, and I have no comment. This was not within my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For my money, that is not responsive to the question, but I'll move on, I think. You've spoken of other discussions you had with politicians as grounding your final opinion. Do we have available notes or records of these conversations that you had, please?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are working notes of official nature. There are my reports to the defence minister about the outcome of my meetings, but all that is at the Defence Ministry, and it is within their purview. But I am naming specific names and I'm quoting dates and I'm telling you what the discussions were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what we want to know, or what the Judges may want to know is how it is you formed this view of a pre-planned -- of a plan to destroy the former Yugoslavia. Take us to your best bit of evidence. Tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, in 1993, a strategic concept of the US and the national Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military doctrine that I mentioned yesterday were endorsed. That is practically a military statute, military constitution of a state. I'm not quoting now, but it says that the entire territory of the planet is an area of vital interest of the USA, and furthermore, the US will protect those interests using military force. Then in 1997, the Balkans were proclaimed to be an area of vital interest to the US. Furthermore, starting with January 1998, the tone of conversation in all negotiations has changed. I met with Mr. Slocum, Mr. Warner -- I can name other names. And if we look at the Kosovo situation which was a matter of general conversation in 1997, in 1998 two main thrusts became crystal clear. One option: Either Milosevic will accept the ultimatum and then we proceed one way; or second option, he doesn't and then the military operation is inevitable. On a different level, we observed a build-up of military activity, an increase in the combat readiness of armed forces, and the observation of the entire military complex indicated to us that preparations were underway to unleash a war. In addition to that. We received information from various sources that corroborated this conclusion. Furthermore, this plan, this doctrine envisaged methods of conducting psychological operations, including military warfare, and all this is clear from those military documents that were endorsed by the US and NATO. In addition to that, there were many, many international conferences discussing a wide variety of aspects. And I am not ruling out the huge role played by operative information. I can draw your attention to the 35th Munich conference in January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think perhaps that is enough. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, from -- I asked you for your best evidence. I take it this is. Now, this, the 1993 strategic concept of the US and the national military document, no doubt you can provide these documents for us if we want them, can we, or tell us where we can get them off a website?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's on the Internet. I don't know the exact website, but these are open-source documents. The whole world has seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are we to take it that if we read this document with an ordinary intelligent, if we are, intelligent mind, we're going to read in it a plan to take over the former -- to destroy the former Yugoslavia? Is this what we're going to find? I just want to know.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take those documents as a manual for action and you look at the way things developed around Kosovo, you will conclude, I think, that everything developed exactly in the way described in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So because we're not -- I should have asked you this as well. I've asked you about intercepts, but I meant to ask you, does your opinion relay -- rely in any way on written communications passing between Western leaders of which you've had sight? Just yes or no. If so, tell us what they are.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please specify. What leaders do you mean? The correspondence and communication between whom and whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's your theory, and you've managed to weave in NATO and all the Western world along with America, but let's focus on America. Have you got any -- have you seen any correspondence coming from or going to American leaders going to show this early plan to destroy the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't. But even if I had seen such a thing, I would not be able to tell you that here. It is a state secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... again. I see. So you wouldn't trust the Judges with it.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't have the right to. If I did, I would be subject to criminal prosecution either in my own country or in the US.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sometimes it's a bit difficult to ask this question because even saying something in a negative is a bit wicked, but can you actually tell the Judges that there was no such material and then we can move on? There was no such material, no written material of the kind to support your theory; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I will quote to you from a published document. It is a report of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, speaking of the military doctrine from 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was asking is this a document which you can hand over to the Court, the one that you're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not today. I can't do it today, quite simply. But this is a published, open-source document. Somebody's trying to catch me out in an untruth here, and -- will you allow me to quote from this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, General, you said it's public. If it's public, why can't it be handed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I physically don't have it. But it's on the Internet. I can refer to a sentence pronounced by Mr. Kissinger, published in the Newsweek magazine. I just don't have that issue of the magazine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you reading from, then? What would you be reading from? I thought you had some document in front of you from which you were going to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While preparing for this hearing, I simply noted down some excerpts and brought them with me, because this is my first participation in a hearing. I thought that a quotation, a reference, would suffice. I have numbers of orders and dates referring to Yugoslavia and orders issued to the Pristina Corps. I have excerpts from them, but I don't have the orders themselves. I can give you references to them, but I don't have the documents as such. They were secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in preparing this witness, either you or your associates should have made it clear to him that those documents might have been needed by the Court. Therefore, they should have been made available. This goes to the management of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have no need to prepare the cross-examination by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wasn't speaking about the -- I'm not speaking about the cross-examination. I'm speaking about the preparation of your own case. It's your preparation of your case that's being called into question now, and that is leading to a waste of the Court's time. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- as far as I'm concerned, if he's reading a narration --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If he wishes to read from what he's written down from an open-source document, then providing that he or the accused, and it's on the accused's shoulders to do this, produces a document in due course, I don't mind him telling us what it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, General. Let us hear what you noted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I just spoke about a moment ago, about the military doctrine. "The US bear global responsibility for everything going on in the world." The question arises in my head: Why the US? Why not the UN? Why not some international organisation? "The US bears global responsibility in all areas of the world that need protecting by military force," and so on. So the US sets objectives, in 1997, proclaiming the Balkans an area of vital interest to the US and go on to take specific decisions. I can read out from a document concerning Rambouillet. Henry Kissinger, Newsweek magazine, May 1999. He says: "New world disorder. The first decision was to send 30.000 troops to Yugoslavia, a country that was not in war with NATO. Second decision envisaged the use of the Serbian refusal of the ultimatum, which was predictable, as a pretext for bombing. Furthermore, despite common belief in Rambouillet, there were no negotiations, there was an ultimatum." That was said by Henry Kissinger, published in Newsweek magazine in May 1999. And furthermore, he says that "The US administration consciously violated its commitment to the UN Charter and international procedures." Was that sufficient? I can continue quoting. I can quote from orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you for your best evidence, and it's very helpful. You've set -- you've told us about something in 1997, and your general concern that the United States bears global responsibility for everything in the world. And then we go back to your 1993 strategic concept, and the national military doctrine. And I just wanted to ask you one question about that. You told us yesterday that the relevant psychological campaign document was FM33-5, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to tell us what year that was published in.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was published somewhat earlier. I will try to find this information now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would 1962 be about right?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, this is an official document of the US army --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Ivasov --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and this document is updated on a yearly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but nevertheless, the version you were referring to was the 1962 version. And this may all show that the United States has been planning the destruction of the former Yugoslavia for three or four Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. decades, but I want to know. The 1962 doctrine, the 1993 strategic concept, the 1997 proclamation that you tell us about, and the Newsweek interview with Mr. Kissinger, now, this is your best evidence. Is there anything else you would like to rely on for proof of the plan to destroy the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to tell you, Mr. Robinson, that this distortion of somebody's evidence is below any human dignity. What Mr. Nice is doing is entirely impermissible with respect to any witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have stopped you. What he's doing is entirely proper. He's testing evidence given in examination-in-chief, and it is open to him to do that. That is an ordinary process in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, I'd like your assistance with some matters that relate specifically to this trial. Do you have any evidence going to show the Americans in league with Mr. Kucan? Kucan. See, the accused has really accused Mr. Kucan as leading to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, and I'm wondering if you have any information that he did this at the Americans' behest?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first of all let me answer your previous question concerning FM33-5 document. All documents of the army tend to have long-term nature. However, on a yearly basis, they are amended, meaning that the basis remains unchanged, and every year or every other year certain amendments are made. This is a tradition in every army. As for your other question, I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And help us, please, because there's a sort of progression in the break-up of the former Yugoslavia. Did you have any evidence going to show that the United States of America was in league with the president of Croatia, leading to him taking his country away from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm giving evidence on issues concerning which I have knowledge. Yesterday, I said that I would be testifying about the Kosovo tragedy. If you have any questions concerning Kosovo, then I will give you an answer. The head of the terrorist organisation, for example, Thaci and Ceku not only were not arrested but were invited to all international conferences where they were a negotiating side. It is a rule that terrorists are not allowed to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, you were asked quite specifically by this accused questions about the role of the United States and the plan to destroy the former Yugoslavia, and I'm testing that evidence. It may be you want to withdraw your evidence. If you do, we will move on. Or do you still maintain that the United States had a plan going back to the mid or early 1990s to destroy the former Yugoslavia? Do you still maintain that?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not state in the courtroom that the United States had in the mid-1990s a plan to destroy the entire Yugoslavia. What I said was that there was a plan on the break-up of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which remained after the major break-up, and my evidence pertained to Kosovo. I can confirm that. I have convictions, and I have evidence to prove that. I just quoted the words of a prominent US statesman, Henry Kissinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, on one matter of detail, I notice the accused yesterday said in the course of an exchange with the Trial Chamber that it was because you knew such information that you weren't allowed to leave Russia for a long time. It's on page 18. Was the accused right in saying that, that you were not allowed to leave Russia because you held such secure information?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. In accordance with the Russian law, a person in possession of highly confidential information is not allowed to travel abroad for up to five years. I left my office in June of 2001, and it wasn't until August, and in relation to my involvement with this trial, was I issued a passport to travel abroad. So since June of 2001, I never travelled abroad. I have never travelled abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And all of the sensitive information that kept you at home or kept you in Russia specifically related to the subject matter of this trial or was it sensitive information generally?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dealt not only with Kosovo. I visited 57 countries of the world where I took part in negotiations and met with presidents, ministers of defence, ministers of foreign affairs, and I was in possession of a huge amount of information. In addition to that, I had access to highly confidential information gathered by our intelligence services. In addition to that, I participated in meetings, consultations with the president, with high government officials within the Ministry of Defence, and as a rule, such information is considered classified. This is a rule that applies to all countries. And there are very strict rules as to who is allowed to make such information public. This rule applies in all democratic countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, now. Your -- it wasn't quite clear yesterday; your detailed dealings with the former Yugoslavia start at what date?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became involved in October of 1996. However, as many things were quite new to me, I did not strictly focus on Bosnian conflict and the Dayton Agreement. I can even tell you that my subordinates were representatives in NATO, Colonel General Zavarski [phoen], for example, and even our generals served as deputies of the Supreme Commander of NATO forces in Europe; General Clark. My subordinate was Mr. Clark's deputy dealing with the Dayton agreement. And from there, we received information that back in January 1998, there were arrows on the maps on General Clark's table, pointing towards Kosovo. This is an information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just try and deal with things, broadly speaking, chronologically. You obviously then know no detail. You weren't involved in the detail of what happened in 1993 -- 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, or 1995, were you?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not take direct participation in those events, but in my capacity, my official capacity and based on various investigative work, I became aware of such information. However, I cannot give evidence concerning that. I can only rely on public information. I did not take part in those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but I'm just going to seek your guidance on this: You will know, of course -- it's back to this -- it's back to this issue, General, if how governments and military try and eavesdrop on each other all the time. The Russian and the Serbian intelligence services formed very close liaison in about 1993, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the period starting in October 1996, but even better, let us start from January 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know that's your period of knowledge, but -- of detailed knowledge, to which I'm going to come, but I'm just checking through you, because I'm sure you know this. As a matter of fact, the Russian and Serbian intelligence and counter-intelligence services, very closely connected as at about 1993 with the man Stanisic playing a role, for example.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I object to this type of qualification. I cannot confirm that. What I spoke about was the cooperation between Russian and Yugoslav special services only pertaining to combat with terrorist organisations, which is something that the whole world is dealing with nowadays, including us. The United States, NATO, and we cooperate concerning that issue, a fight against terrorism. I can confirm that, that we had very close cooperation, very fruitful cooperation on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The way governments all listen in on each other, just help us with this because we're very concerned about Srebrenica. Did you carry out intercepts of Yugoslavia, Belgrade, and of this accused, you Russians? Did you?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I knew much. However, in every country, not all highly placed officials have access to all of the information. Not even President knows everything. Therefore, to claim that I was involved in this is something that I refuse to do. I don't think that this is the key point for this evidence, whether I as witness took part in intercepting conversations. I don't think that any state would disclose such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I clarify this: General, before you came to The Hague, I understand that you had got permission from your government, in one way or another, to give evidence in relation to the Kosovo indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And not in relation to Bosnian and Croatian indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not defined or ordered by the government. I myself clarified that I would testify only about the period and events that I am well familiar with. This was not prescribed by my government. However, I couldn't have envisaged the questions put by Mr. Nice. This kind of information is held by secret services. Nobody gave me permission to disclose that, but I didn't even ask for such permission, because I did not expect such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you are suggesting that you are not in a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. position to answer any question in relation to Bosnian and Croatian indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, Your Honour, I can only speak in general terms. I can speak of the implementation of the Dayton agreement because there was a Russian brigade deployed there. And also in Mons, in Shape [phoen], in NATO we had our representative. So this is something that I can discuss. However, I did not take part in Dayton negotiations and I have little information concerning that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had meetings with the leaders of the Republic of Serbia. I visited that region. However, the questions put to me by Mr. Nice is not something that I can tell you about, about what was going on in Srebrenica region. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not Republic of Serbia but Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, General, I certainly wasn't going to ask you for any detail but as you will appreciate from my very first observation to you today the Prosecution in this case is the servant and supporter of no one. We are trying to find out the truth, and since you hold the office you do, I just wanted to know if, in Russia, there is likely to be material in the form of intercepted conversations of Belgrade and this accused that may help us. I suspect you could answer. Do they hold such material?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I hope that your goal is to seek objective truth. However, to this day, we have still not broken codes from the Second World War. And for some reason, you focus your efforts on attempts to disclose the secrets of Russian secret service and their technical services. This is the topmost secret in every country. Great Britain has not yet disclosed methods and mechanisms used to break German codes during World War II despite the fact that the Nuremberg trials have been concluded. And I'm really surprised that you're focusing on this issue, the issue of intercepts. I have a lot of information from other sources. This is not the main issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, General, the problem may be that you've chosen to rely on some material from intercepts in relation to Kosovo and that therefore the issue of intercepts has opened up as an issue in the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me clarify once again that wiretapping of terrorists is a legal activity in any state, and what was intercepted while wiretapping the conversations of terrorists is something that I can tell you about, the bit that is known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm going to move on from that, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know if I've interrupted Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to the period of your particular knowledge and seek your assistance. Listening to your evidence yesterday provided a clear picture, but correct me if I've got it wrong, of KLA terrorists being resisted by a totally lawful and well-behaved Serbian government. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if you'd help us, please, with some comments on workings of the Contact Group. Now, you know about the Contact Group, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, just to remind the Court, the Contact Group had a Russian representative on it; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, the Contact Group was not authorised by the UN Security Council or any other international legal body. This was something like a voluntary international conference, and Russia takes part in numerous international conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we take it that the sort of information available to you, General, would have been equally available to your representative on the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that. I did not take part in the meetings of the Contact Group. This is something that the services within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia were involved in. I simply analysed documents that were adopted within the Contact Group and adopted only as recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you are looking for that, I can tell you, Mr. Nice, that on the 9th of March, 1998, in London, the Contact Group, I'm quoting: "Acknowledged the presence of terrorist structures in Kosovo, condemned terrorism and separatism, condemned upon the proposal of Russia the forces funding training and arming terrorist groups." This statement was issued on the 9th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quoted from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- I'm so grateful because you've obviously written that down in advance of coming here in order that you could read it out, and of course we're going to find that, because from time to time Russia made separate decisions within the Contact Group. Now, you came with that particular quotation. I'll ask --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about independent decisions or separate decisions taken by Russia within the Contact Group. I would ask you to refrain from such claims pertaining to Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would the Chamber be good enough to take a collection of documents, which will be a new exhibit, available for distribution with an index on the front. We probably can display them on the overhead projector. I'm going to read some, but I hope a limited number of these, and the Chamber will, I imagine, be pleased to know that I'm sure I can conclude my examination of this witness today and it won't be necessary for him to come back and I shan't be asking for him to bring any documents in light of the answers he's already given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we -- now, General, I'm sorry that this isn't translated into Russian, but I wasn't to know what you were going to be going to say in evidence when you came. And if the usher would be good enough, we'll go through the materials and I'll describe them to you. And if the usher would press the appropriate screen on the television. It's already done. You can either look at the document, which will be in English on your left, or you can view it on the screen which will be in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is impermissible to give to the witness documents in a language he doesn't understand. He should be able to read the document, and this is not how a witness should be treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's going to be placed on the ELMO and will be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what if it's on the ELMO? The document cannot be translated in its entirety. There are 50 pages here. And bearing in mind the manipulations of Mr. Nice and taking out words out of context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a permissible comment, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it is not appropriate to give to the witness documents in a language he doesn't understand. That should be completely clear to you. This is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how much of this document are you going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are several passages that I wish to read, but I'll read them generously. It is simply impossible, if we have speakers of languages other than the languages of the institution to forecast in advance and find the resources to prepare documents like this not knowing what the accused will say. I should respectfully remind the accused through the Court that all the documents he produced through the previous witness were provided in the Russian language, without any translated version for us. Not that I rely on that as -- in itself as a justification for what I'm doing. What I'm doing is clearly the best and appropriate policy under the Statute and regulations which requires documents to be in the language of the institution. I'm glad to have made the accused laugh.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Naturally. The Russian language is an official language of the United Nations, and you have no interpreters for Russian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And even in the NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice and the witness, we are going to take an adjournment now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have noted the objection that you have made to this document being put to the witness without it being translated in his language. However, as indicated by Mr. Nice, he only intends to put particular passages from the document to the witness. Those will be translated by the interpreter. If the witness finds that he's at a disadvantage, then it is a matter for him to bring that to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. attention of the Chamber. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, incidentally, I'm told by the interpreters that because of the particular circumstances of interpretation, I'm going to have to speak more loudly or closer to the microphone. So if I appear to be shouting, it's not a reflection of any attitude, it's merely an administrative necessity. So I hope you won't be offended. Your previous -- thank you. Your previous observation about the role of the Contact Group, I must respectfully suggest, is incorrect. For example, in his report to the Security Council of the 30th of April of 1998, a document which, if is isn't an exhibit I will have copied and provided, the Secretary-General said: "I have had to rely on information and assessments provided by the Contact Group, OSCE and the European Union, as foreseen in paragraph 16 of Security Council Resolution 1160." So, General, the Contact Group served an important and formal function for the Secretary-General and the United Nations. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree insofar as the Contact Group sometimes made good conclusions for the benefit of the General-Secretary and provided recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was on the basis of that report, again a document if not already an exhibit I'll produce it, on the basis of that report that United Nations Resolution 1199 was made, which led to the October agreements, and do you accept, General, that within that Resolution the United Nations acknowledged gratefully statements of the foreign ministers made by France, Germany, Italy, and the Russian Federation as well as the United Kingdom, USA, and other countries?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you could specify, what statements do you have in mind, and what is the agreement you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is Resolution 1199, which led to the October agreements with which the KVM was concerned to verify. I do not have the Russian statement, but this Resolution included within it gratitude for a statement from the Russian Federation.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I acknowledge the Contact Group with respect. However, the Security Council took into account -- took into account its recommendations and opinion but not only, not only the opinion of the Contact Group. If you speak about the October agreement, do you mean the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement of October 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now move to the collection of documents from the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the usher would display them, although I shall ask him, so that people can see what we have, to display them in sequence rapidly, we will stop at only a limited number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Ivasov, the documents we have, so you can know what is going to the Judges, is a statement on Kosovo of the Contact Group foreign ministers dated the 24th of September, 1997. Next page is blank. The following page is a statement on Kosovo of the 25th of February, 1998, and that's available. The following page is blank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I would be grateful if you would bear in mind that I do not know the English language. I speak German, by the way, so I cannot comment on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I seek no comment on the ones I've mentioned. It's just simply for completeness, revealing what we have. There is then a Security Council note or letter of the 12th of March, 1998. Just display that. And immediately following that, we have the letter, I think, or the annex to which you referred. So the next page is headed "Annex," and it refers to a meeting in London on the 9th of March of 1998, and I'm going to read several paragraphs from it at a speed, General, that I hope will be acceptable to the interpreters and to you. Three lines down on paragraph number 2 reads as follows -- and any interpreter who finds I'm going too fast, please wave at me or something. "We are dismayed that in the period since September, rather than taking steps to reduce tension or to enter without pre-conditions into dialogue towards a political solution, the Belgrade authorities have applied repressive measures in Kosovo. We note with particular concern the recent violence in Kosovo, resulting in at least 80 fatalities, and condemn the use of excessive force by Serbian police against civilians, and against peaceful demonstrators in Pristina on the 2nd of March. "Our condemnation of the actions of the Serbian police should not in any way be mistaken for an endorsement of terrorism. Our position on this is clear: We wholly condemn terrorist actions by the Kosovo Liberation Army or any other group or individual. Those in the Kosovo Albanian community who speak for the different political constituencies should make it clear that they, too, abhor terrorism. We insist, likewise, that those outside the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who are supplying finance, arms, or training for terrorist activity in Kosovo should immediately cease doing so. "We condemn the large-scale police actions of the last 10 days that further inflamed an already volatile situation. The violent repression of non-violent expression of political views is completely indefensible. We call upon the authorities in Belgrade to invite independent forensic experts to investigate the very serious allegations of extrajudicial killings. If these accusations are borne out, we expect the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to prosecute and punish those responsible." I omit paragraph 5. Paragraph 6: "In the light of the deplorable violence in Kosovo, we feel compelled to take steps to demonstrate to the authorities in Belgrade that they cannot defy international standards without facing severe consequences." Over the page, please. At the top: "Against that background, the Contact Group requests a mission to Kosovo by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, urges the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia to begin gathering information related to the violence in Kosovo that may fall within its jurisdiction." And then halfway down the page: "Will continue vigorously to support the efforts of Sant 'Egidio to secure implementation of the Education agreement ..." Over the page, please, to page 4. And I said I would draw these passages to your attention, or at least some of them. Towards the bottom of the page: "The Contact Group notes that the Russian Federation cannot support measures (c) and (d) above," which we can see set out, "but if there is no progress towards the steps taken -- the steps called for by the Contact Group, the Russian Federation will then be willing to discuss all the above measures. "We call upon President Milosevic to take rapid and effective steps to stop the violence and engage in a commitment to find a political solution to the issue of Kosovo through dialogue. Specifically, he should within 10 days: "Withdraw the Special Police Units and cease action by security forces affecting the civilian population; "Allow access to Kosovo for the Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations as well as by representatives of the Contact Group and other embassies; "Commit himself publicly to begin a process of dialogue, along the lines of paragraph 10, with the leadership of the Kosovo Albanian community; "Cooperate in a constructive manner with the Contact Group in the implementation of the actions specified in paragraph 6 above which require urgent action by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Over the page and, Your Honours, this is the only one that I'm going to read at this length. "If President Milosevic --" Top of the page, please. "If President Milosevic takes these steps, we will immediately reconsider the measures we have now adopted. If he fails to take these steps, and repression continues in Kosovo, the Contact Group will move to further international measures and specifically to pursue a freeze on the funds held abroad by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbian governments." Paragraph 8: "Belgrade's own actions have seriously set back the process of normalisation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's relations with the international community. Unless the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia takes steps to resolve the serious political and human rights issues in Kosovo, there is no prospect of any improvement in its international standing. On the other hand, the concrete proposals to resolve the serious political and human rights issues in Kosovo will improve the international position of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and prospects for normalisation of its international relationships and full rehabilitation in international institutions." Paragraph 10, finally: "The way to defeat terrorism in Kosovo is for Belgrade to offer the Kosovo Albanian community a genuine political process. The authorities in Belgrade and the leadership of the Kosovo Albanian community must assume their responsibility to enter without pre-conditions into a meaningful dialogue on political status issues. The Contact Group stands ready to facilitate such a dialogue." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, General, you, I think, came to court with a passage from this noted that dealt simply with the use of the term "terrorism." Having heard the majority of the text read to you, and bearing in mind that you acknowledged that Russia's member of the Contact Group had access to the same material that you had, would you like to accept that this document by the Contact Group is a fair representation of what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection is this: The question was not put in an appropriate manner, because it was precisely in sub-item (c) that says -- (c) and (d), rather, that repressive actions of security forces of Yugoslavia in Kosovo are mentioned. And it says further below that the Contact Group notes that the Russian Federation cannot support measures (c) and (d). Therefore, the Russian Federation did not actually support this qualification about repressive measures, because if you remember, gentlemen, speaking of those 80 fatalities, it was the clash in Prekaze, where a terrorist group headed by Adem Jashari was liquidated after several days of shooting with the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'll ask Mr. Nice to reply, but (c) and (d) deals with denial of visas and a moratorium and the question that he asked was whether the witness was prepared to accept that the document was a fair representation of what was happening on the ground. That is, the activities on the ground. So I don't see any relationship between that and the fact that Russia did not accept sub-item (c) and (d). The witness should answer if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this document was to a great extent a result of compromise amongst various parties, and the fact that Russia did not agree to two subparagraphs involving accusations or conclusions does not mean that it was not a valid document. But it is a fact that the Russian Federation, the Ministry of Defence, and myself welcomed any attempt by any political structure to find a peaceful settlement. And specifically, a peaceful settlement of the Kosovo problem. I do support this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, I'm interrupting you. Mr. Nice, rephrase your question and clarify precisely what you mean by "activities on the ground."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. But I'm grateful to the witness for his last answer in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, General Ivasov, as I say, you brought to us an extract that referred simply to terrorist activity, which I think we can see in paragraph 3 of this annex. I've read out a general account of tensions, of condemnation of terrorism, of condemnation of large-scale police actions over the last ten days, of deplorable violence in Kosovo, and so on, and I'm going to suggest to you that the Contact Group, on all the best available information, had set out in an evenhanded way the situation on the ground. Do you disagree with that or do you accept that that is what they had done?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the Contact Group was not an officially established body, and its conclusions were sometimes subjective. Second, you read out the paragraphs that were agreed upon. However, the proposals of the Russian delegate, one of which was not to give visas to KLA leaders, to arrest terrorists upon arrival to Western capitals, as well as a number of other proposals, were not accepted and are not reflected, therefore, in this document. Then, Mr. Nice, you speak very confidently about certain matters such as repression, et cetera. And I'm telling you once again that Russia welcomed and proposed the complex of measures for political settlement, and it did, therefore, take part in Contact Group -- in the Contact Group and other bodies. But on a parallel track to this political process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered the question. Just pay attention to the question. The question was whether you agree that the Contact Group had set out in an evenhanded way the situation on the ground relating to the activities that took place on the ground, and you're asked to say whether you disagreed with that or whether you accept it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not accept it completely, because the Contact Group was not in a position to give an objective evaluation. It issued agreed-upon recommendations. There were points on which there was no agreement and Russian proposals that were not included. So to agree with this document in entirety is something that I cannot do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have the answer now, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, it is not true that Russian delegate agreed upon the items on (a) and (b); i.e., a comprehensive arms embargo and refusal to supply equipment to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Russian delegate did agree to these paragraphs. My personal opinion was somewhat different, but it was not taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll move on. If the usher could help, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, which we won't linger on, is the letter of the 27th of March. The following page, just for display, is the annex. Perhaps I can just look at this very briefly, or couple of passages on this. We see under paragraph 2, General Ivasov, that under this annex of the meeting of the 25th of March of 1998, it's recorded that: "In London, the group called upon President Milosevic to take rapid and effective steps to end the violence in Kosovo and commit himself to a political solution through unconditional dialogue." And that the group adopted a plan to advance these goals. And at paragraph 5 it recorded that: "Since our meeting in London there has been progress in some areas of concern, notably some movement in Belgrade's position on dialogue on a range of issues, including the autonomy of Kosovo and the conclusions of the long-overdue agreement on implementation of the education accord." If you would be good enough, Usher, to take us to the next page. Just taking, I hope, appropriate selections from a long document. Paragraph 9 sets out how: "Unless the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia takes steps to resolve the serious political and human rights issues in Kosovo, there is no prospect of any improvement in its international standing." Going down to paragraph 10. The group reaffirmed its "Strong opposition to all terrorist" -- my emphasis -- "to terrorist actions. Violence does not contribute to the search for a solution in Kosovo. This applies equally to Serbian police and Kosovar Albanian extremists." Paragraph 10 welcomes Dr. Rugova's clear commitment to non-violence and urges others to follow that leadership. It goes on to say: "Belgrade authorities cannot, however, justify their repression and violence in Kosovo in the name of anti-terrorist activities. We repeat that the way to combat terrorism is for Belgrade to offer the Kosovar Albanian community a genuine political process." And at paragraph 13 the group explains its fundamental position as remaining the same. "We support neither independence nor the maintenance of the status quo as the end result of negotiations between Belgrade authorities and the Kosovo Albanian leadership on the status of Kosovo."
