So I realise to save time I've only read some extracts, but do you have any challenge to the passages I've read out of that particular document?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I support, and I did participate in the drafting of several paragraphs of this document, but I wish to emphasise once again, the Russian representative, just as all the others, were unofficial participants. However, I do not support the conclusions referring to repression and violence as applied to terrorists. I have a different position, and I have stated it many times, including to the readership of Yugoslavia. It was the position of the defence ministry. I said it was necessary to be more active in making arrests and neutralising the leaders of terrorist organisations in order to minimise casualties among the civilian population. In other words, I agree with some of the conclusions and don't agree with the others. But you have to bear in mind that the Russian representative was not an official representative, just as the Contact Group was not an official body itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you've made that point several times.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very useful, though, in reaching a peaceful settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nice. For the benefit of the transcript, I would like to check whether the witness had really said that he supported and he did participate in the drafting of several paragraphs of this document. Did you say so? You did participate in the drafting of several paragraphs of this document or you said you did not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did participate as an expert, as an expert. And I made suggestions only on the issue of building up measures of political solution. That was my position and the position held by the Russian defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So that your colleague and all those on the Contact Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Group had the real benefit of your input, General, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next page, please, is the letter of the 30th of April. And one passage from -- if you could just display that. It's the letter sending -- and then we see the following page, the annex. There's only one paragraph for comment. Paragraph 3: "The Contact Group condemns the increase in violence in recent days in Kosovo. In particular, the excessive use of force by the Yugoslav army and the proliferation of arms in the territory. The Contact Group absolutely rejects terrorism as a means of bringing about political change, as well as all other violence to suppress political dissent. The Contact Group calls upon political leaders in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in the countries of the region to exercise maximum restraint, full respect for human rights, and to prevent the introduction of arms and of armed groups from outside, and to condemn terrorism." General Ivasov, an entirely fair position for the Contact Group to have taken?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on the entire document because I don't have it in front of me, but as for condemning terrorism and putting an end to the arms supply and the increasing of terrorist activity, yes, those segments I do support. But as for the use of excessive force, this is phrased in general terms. I said yesterday, and I can confirm today that Russia and its military delegations discussed in detail with their Yugoslav counterparts the use of military force in fight with terrorists. I can tell you that I saw a number of orders limiting the activity of military troops, and I can give you the numbers of those orders. Within the military, there is military prosecutor's office and military court. So those who violate military law and disobey orders can be prosecuted. Such courts existed, and there were trials against violators, and I can tell you that I'm sure that law was applied in cases where excessive force was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're repeating what you told us yesterday, and of course if there is going to be evidence of these prosecutions we'll see it in due course, but perhaps you'd just help us with this: Within this period, 1998, were you yourself in Kosovo at all at any time?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: During what period of time?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, no, I was not in Kosovo. My officers were there, the officers who reported back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next letter, please, Usher, is the 24th of June of 1998. And then the annex which follows it. If we could display that. The annex at 3 is what I will read, and possibly paragraph 6. From the 12th of June meeting reads as follows: "Security forces have again intervened indiscriminately, causing many civilian casualties and forcing tens of thousands of inhabitants to flee their homes. Ministers condemned Belgrade's massive and disproportionate use of force, which has resulted in widespread destruction and the deliberate displacement of large numbers of people. They also condemned the failure by Belgrade to take concrete steps to reduce tensions. Ministers therefore decided to put the authorities in Belgrade a set of essential points on which they required immediate action to prevent any further deterioration in the situation. These cover concrete measures:" and then set out: "To cease all actions by the security forces affecting the civilian population and order the withdrawal of security units used for civilian repression; "To enable effective and continuous international monitoring in Kosovo and allow unimpeded access for monitors; "To facilitate an agreement with the office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the Red Cross the full return to their homes of refugees and displaced persons and to allow free and unimpeded access for humanitarian organisations and supplies to Kosovo; "To make rapid progress in the dialogue with Kosovo Albanian leadership." And if the usher would be good enough to take us to the following page. That's paragraph 6 and 7. "Ministers expect that Belgrade will take the steps set out in paragraph 3 above immediately. They welcomed the invitation by President Yeltsin to President Milosevic to a meeting on 16th of June. They stressed the importance to President Milosevic taking advantage of that meeting to announce progress on the above steps and to commit Belgrade to their -- to their implementation in full. If the steps set out in paragraph 3 are not taken without delay, there will be moves to adopt further measures to halt the violence and protect the civilian population, including those that may require the authorisation of a Security Council resolution." Paragraph 7: "In the meantime, ministers also urged the International Criminal Tribunal to undertake investigation, agreed to give active support to UNHCR, and undertook efforts to assist neighbouring countries to improve their security." General, this meeting of the Contact Group is acting on the basis of information including that which came from you and your offices. Is there any reason to doubt the depiction it gives of the position in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our representatives within the Contact Group received this information and, to a certain extent, passed it on. However, we closely followed how the Yugoslav side was implementing the recommendation, and I will read you two brief lines: "The order of the commander of the Pristina Corps, number 45520. Ensure a high level of responsibility of all servicemen of the Yugoslav army with respect to issued orders. All violators to face action and prosecution." A directive of the General Staff was issued signed by General Ojdanic about the measures of servicemen in the territory where there was terrorist activity. Where it is stated that "killing the persons who were imprisoned, wounding them, was prohibited without previous court order." This also refers to civilian population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. I'm stopping you, General. There seems to be a pattern in your answers which is to provide information which does not relate to the question that was asked. It's perhaps a lawyer-like practice, and I don't say so in a disparaging manner, being a lawyer myself, but please attend to the specific question asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that. Normally I apply my new rule, which is not try, try and try again, but try, try, and give up. I think this time I'll move on after my first attempt because we've got quite a lot of material to cover. If the usher would take us to the next letter, which is the letter of the 6th of July. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the question was not put properly with regard to the quotation. Mr. Nice quoted item 3 of this annex and failed to quote item 4, which basically balances out item 3, and it says there that ministers expect Kosovo Albanian leadership to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a classic example of how you can re-examine. You can re-examine on that and put it to the witness, Mr. Milosevic. That's a classical function of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm telling this to you, because everything that was done by the Contact Group - and we have evidence of that in these papers - was to balance out the action of legal forces and the action of terrorists. Nowadays, nobody in this world would do something like that. Would you imagine a statement nowadays where it would be stated that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've -- I've stopped you because you're going beyond the permissible limit of a comment. It is open to you to re-examine on this matter, to say to the witness in re-examination, "You have been asked about paragraph 3. Now I'm putting to you the substance of what is in paragraph 4," and that's it, and you would have dealt with the point. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, General, before I move to the next -- and I'm nearly at the end of this exercise -- the next letter, you've been quoting from Pristina Corps documents. Where did you obtain them from, because we've had some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can give you the dates and the numbers of orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you get them?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and both those issued by the Ministry of Defence, the General Staff, and the Pristina Corps. All of these orders were classified. I made excerpts for myself, and these excerpts were brought in to us by Russian representatives in the Verification Mission. Why did they do that? They did that because any analysis must include the analysis of legal documents, orders, legal provisions, and so on, and then follow on to analyse how they were implemented. This is exactly the procedure that Russian representatives followed. I can give you the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe later if time allows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please, Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I would like to hear from you, based on what Mr. Nice has just said, whether Mr. Nice claims Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that they do not have any documents of the Yugoslav army from the time period of NATO aggression against Yugoslavia, meaning orders of Pristina Corps, General Staff, Supreme Command, and so on. Is Mr. Nice claiming that they do not have such documents in their possession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate question for me to put to Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice knows how to manage his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next document, please, Usher, which is, I think, the letter of the 16th of July. Can you put the next document on, please, which is the letter of the 16th of July. Yes, and then the annex. Thank you very much, you're ahead of me as ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I only want to read from the meeting on the 8th of July, paragraph 3, the first bullet point, so it's a bit further down the page. "Contact Group noted that: "The withdrawal of security forces for civilian repression has not yet been carried out, although the security forces have shown some measure of restraint recently; "Rapid progress in the dialogue with the Kosovo Albanian leadership has not been achieved. "The Contact Group acknowledged the significance of the undertakings given by President Milosevic in his meeting with President Yeltsin on the 16th of June and emphasised the need for them to be fully implemented. "It noted President Milosevic's commitment to allow international observers free and unrestricted access to Kosovo ..." I'm not going to read any more, but I'm trying to read a balanced part of all these documents. Are you happy with that part of the document?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I gave -- I was against and I still am against an equal treatment of legal authorities and terrorists. There was no analysis of any laws, regulations, and orders. None of that was done. Therefore, for me to evaluate and give you a yes or no answer is very difficult, especially since I do not see the document in its entirety. Each item, each paragraph of the documents of the Contact Group is a compromise of either the preceding paragraph or the subsequent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're all available to be considered in full, and we'll come just to the conclusion of this bundle of documents. Just so that the usher puts them on the page sequentially, we come eventually to the conclusions of the 22nd of January, 1999. And this a meeting on that date. Chairman's conclusions. In the middle that page: "The Contact Group looks to the FRY to stop all offensive actions or repressions in Kosovo; "To promote the safe return home of those persons displaced in the past few days from the Racak area and to take all steps to avoid a humanitarian catastrophe; "Permit the KVM and its chief of mission to carry out their responsibilities unimpeded; "To cooperate fully with the ICTY, in particular ... access to investigators; "To work with the Tribunal to ensure that those responsible for Racak are brought to justice; "To suspend those VJ or MUP officers operating in Racak on the 15th of January pending the results of the investigation ...; "And to comply fully with OSCE/FRY and NATO/FRY agreements ..." And if we then go over, please, Usher, to the next document I'll ask a compendious question, which I think is a letter of the 29th of January followed by an annex in two pages. And if you'd go to the second page of the annex, we see a list of demands by the Contact Group that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia stop offensive action, comply with agreements and resolutions, promote the safe return of those forced to flee, cooperate with the OSCE and the KVM, cooperate with this Tribunal, investigate Racak, suspend certain officers and police. And there we are. Now, that's records of the Contact Group at the end of the period where it made those demands on Yugoslavia. Those simply reflected, did they not, General, a combination of events with repression and excesses revealed by the forces of Yugoslavia as well as terrorist activity or however so described by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is difficult for me to answer Mr. Nice's questions. First of all, I don't know what the position was of the Russian side and its proposals. I was not a direct participant in these events. And the third is that these are not official documents. Therefore, it is very difficult for me now to give an assessment of this large set of documents. I can answer specific questions, but I cannot answer questions of these nature that require a very extensive analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case my last question on this topic is as follows: You explained in answer to His Honour Judge Kwon and to me that you had been really fully engaged in drafting one of these reports and that your -- and your office's information had been available to the Contact Group at that time. Did that continue throughout the period of the Contact Group so that your input was -- and your office's input was available at all times to the Contact Group through the Russian representative?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I did not say that I was a full participant. Either there was a mistake in -- in interpretation or there was some other misunderstanding there. I said that I took part in drafting some of the documents as an expert. As for your second question, the officers of the Verification Mission supplied information to the Contact Group, and I can tell you right away that they did not do that. They reported back to their superiors, and then that information was compiled together, and as such it could have been sent either to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or elsewhere and thus reach the representative. I don't know exactly what was the extent of the information that he received. No officers of the Russian army ever supplied any information to the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move to give exhibit numbers to the Contact Group material, I can provide for you, if it would be helpful, and have marked as exhibits the report I relied on of the Secretary-General of the 30th of April, where he refers to the role of the Contact Group. That hasn't yet been produced in evidence. I can also produce Resolution 1199, which leads up to the October agreement, and that hasn't been produced in evidence. They are now available. So that if they were all to be produced, the sensible course might be to put them in their logical order, which, with your leave, would be first the report, and that's now available for distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we do that, let us hear Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents of the Contact Group have nothing to do with the evidence given by General Ivasov. General Ivasov was not involved with Contact Group. He did not work there. He doesn't even share the assessments of the Contact Group. He did not refer to the documents of the Contact Group, and no documents of the Contact Group can be admitted through this witness. If Mr. Nice wants to tender them, then he should do it through a witness that was involved with the work of the Contact Group, not through General Ivasov. If we applied this procedure, then we could probably tender into evidence the Dutch papers stating or reporting that General Ivasov is in town today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am not in agreement with you, Mr. Milosevic. The witness was able to comment on several passages put to him by Mr. Nice, and it's quite proper for this document to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. May the Security Council report of the 30th of April, 1998, I quoted -- thank you very much. 789.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May Resolution 1199 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 790, and then 791 for the whole bunch of documents with tab 1 to tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, the October agreements were that which KVM monitored, and just to remind everyone, before KVM, as you will probably know, there were various independent KDOM missions, including from Russia, America, England, I think France and some others. Some of those KDOM missions merging into KVM, all of them except for part of the American KDOM mission which remained separate. This is just to remind everybody of evidence we've heard. But because of the position that you take, I just want to check that you will check your observations on some evidence of General Klaus Naumann, the most senior military member of NATO present at the time, and he said that to the best of his knowledge, he thought that the Yugoslav authorities honoured the October agreement because they withdrew their forces to barracks, and this was not an easy thing to do, to bring 6.000 police officers back, and that he explained - this is Klaus Naumann - that they were optimistic at the end of October that they had achieved a breakthrough. Now, let me not mislead you, General Ivasov. You have made some very serious allegations about NATO and about its objectivity and about its complicity and I don't know what. This is what Klaus Naumann said: He says, "Initially the Yugoslav authorities honoured the agreement and were optimistic." Do you think that Klaus Naumann got it right?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Klaus Naumann was right to the extent that Yugoslav authorities did honour their obligations, the demands that were made to them at a diplomatic level but were backed with threats of military force. As early as summer of 1998, Secretary-General of NATO, Mr. Solana, stated Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that all options have been taken into account, and NATO was prepared to mount airstrikes and ground operation. After that, concerning the agreement of the 16th October, he stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that NATO forces were prepared to start strikes within 96 hours. Strikes against Yugoslavia. This was the military pressure applied. I agree with Naumann about the fact that Yugoslav army and Yugoslav leadership even agreed to violate their own sovereignty by allowing NATO planes to conduct reconnaissance in their airspace and on their territory. This is the violation of one country's sovereignty. However, Mr. Milosevic did it in order to avoid military intervention. He agreed to that. And I would like to point to the attention of Their Honours that Yugoslav forces, legal forces, from the summer until fall of 1998 inflicted significant losses to the terrorist organisations. After Yugoslav army and police pulled back to their barracks, the number of terrorist acts in the area increased by four times, and this despite the presence of Verification Mission and air reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, you know, you can, if you like - I'm sure the Judges will prefer this - answer questions previously where they are susceptible to brevity. I was going to come to the matter you've now raised, you see, because Klaus Naumann, representative of this organisation NATO that you characterised in the way you did yesterday, told the Court this, and it's transcript page 6995. He told the Court: "In all fairness, to the best information I got from the reports on the ground from KDOM and later on from the KVM, many of the incidents were triggered by the UCK" -- KLA -- "who obviously tried to exploit the vacuum created by the withdrawn Serb security forces and who then sneaked in to take control of regions or areas. They also, I think, launched provocations, and they were not free of violence in doing so." This is the most senior representative of NATO speaking to this Court. You have not a word of objection to what he said, do you? You'd agree with it.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please specify one thing. I must confess I wasn't quite paying attention, Mr. Nice. I apologise. Just tell me who sneaked into what zones and provoked violence. Did you mean state authorities or the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The KLA into the areas vacated by the forces that were withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had an abundant amount of information to the effect that indeed the terrorist organisation of the Kosovo Liberation Army -- Your Honour, I'll read again from an order. "Albanian terrorist forces have been reorganised, equipped with modern arms --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped you. I've stopped you for the reasons that I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, Klaus Naumann went on, General Klaus Naumann went on to say this, he said: "The problem is that in many cases, as far as I have seen later on, particularly in the course of November and December, the Serb side reacted again in a disproportionate way. It was, if I may say so, the old attitude to react to an incident where perhaps an individual had tried to kill or had killed a police officer." He went on -- so bear that in mind, please, because I want to finish this passage. He went on to say the following things, speaking of NATO, that NATO lacked an instrument, how to get the KLA under control and how to influence them, because he said in his NATO capacity, he was never allowed to talk to the UCK man, the KLA man, or representative because NATO had initially called these people terrorists, and the iron rule was that NATO will never negotiate with terrorists. That's something which is not unimportant if you look at the composition of NATO, he said, since in some NATO countries we have terrorist movements. And then finally, he said that after December they saw increased violence by both sides. Now, this is the man who headed NATO, and I've, of course, summarised the passage of his evidence, but I hope fairly. Is there anything in what I've summarised to you that is not fair and accurate? He was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only respect for General Naumann. I had many discussions with him over the Kosovo problem. He's right in saying that NATO could not do any policing, and that is why we suggested, instead of military pressure, to deploy international police forces, and that is something that Mr. Naumann agreed with. However, there is one important point here. When Mr. Naumann is saying that if one policeman is killed it is not all right to use excessive force in reaction. It was recognised, both within NATO and within the Contact Group, that a terrorist network had been established, a very broad organisation numbering many thousands of armed men. And every terrorist act, such as the murder of a policeman or a peaceful citizen, could not be dealt with by just two policemen. Of course there had to be a reaction. But most of the terrorist acts were wide-scale, massive, well-planned actions. In order to detect terrorists, arrest them, or liquidate them, it was necessary to use major forces, primarily of the security forces but also the army. And I wish to point out one more thing. This is the leadership of the General Staff and official orders which forbid the use of heavy weaponry. Certain particular actions were forbidden under the regulations and the legislation. And based on these orders, we concluded that all the necessary measures were taken to avoid the use of heavy weaponry and to avoid collateral damage to civilian population. But we do not deny that certain excesses could have happened involving individual troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said thank you, General. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now move to the next topic upon which -- I move to the next topic on which you ventured an opinion, namely the accuracy of reporting of the KVM mission which was in the theatre between the late autumn of 1998 and the 20th of March of 1999. Were you yourself there? You weren't there in 1998. Were you there at all yourself before the 20th of March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I occupied a rather high position, and I did not organise any military actions. However, I led military observers. I gave them tasks, and I visited Belgrade very often. I did not have any need to go out directly into the field or visit the areas of combat action or even the area where the mission was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To remind yourself -- to remind you, rather, and to just remind the Chamber if it needs reminding, the KVM reporting system was from field officer or field office up to a coordination centre, to a regional centre, and then to Pristina, for example, and then to Ambassador Walker. We have heard in court, as a Defence witness, somebody who for, I think, two or three weeks ran a field office, a man called Keith. We have some material in the form of regular reporting in documents, and we've heard from people at the regional level, Maisonneuve and Ciaglinski, as well as General Drewienkiewicz, one of Walker's deputies. Tell us, please, again, why it is you say that the reports of which we have heard in evidence are unreliable.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the references I made to several orders and laws were an integral part of the work and the reports of Russian observers. Second, Russian observers always started their work by studying the laws and decisions of the state authorities of whatever region they were sent to. However -- and let me add, they sent their reports to their superior officers. However, in Mr. Walker's reports, you will see no mention, no reference to any analysis of legislation or regulations. Furthermore, Mr. Walker and many other NATO representatives did not analyse the orders issued to the police and the army. How could they make any conclusions about the legal or illegal character of their actions? There is probably a number of other arguments I could make to explain that they did not do their work conscientiously. And the reports they sent to the OSCE did not reflect the objective, the real picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this is a -- I think something different. No complaint, General, but maybe a little different than how you expressed it yesterday. Your concern is that the reports didn't focus on the legislative or regulatory framework of the military or the police. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Prosecution is focusing precisely on officials who held official positions, who issued orders, who made the rules. And when you collect your evidence only by interviewing refugees going to Macedonia or interviewing terrorists, members of the KLA, and accidental passersby, that is also necessary, perhaps. But I, for instance, instructed our observers that they should start their work by interviewing officials, by studying the rules, the regulations, and the legislation of the state authorities and hearing the evidence of the -- of the other party. Obviously Mr. Walker's mission had a different approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again just to remind you, if you weren't aware of this, and to refresh our memories, the mission started off with a large number of military personnel because they were said to be typically more readily available, the intention being, in due course, to transfer to one that would be more built on those with election experience and similar. And the reporting was factual, it was simply to report on what was happening Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on the ground, there being specific lines of communication established with both the Serb forces and with the KLA, thus to get over, for example, the problem that NATO had about dealing with people described as terrorists. And what I want from you, and I don't think you've helped me yet, is I want to know why, and I'm going to hold them up, exhibits of this kind, which are the reports that are in evidence and that I may ask you to look at, why they are not factually reliable. So I don't understand it, what you're saying. Why aren't they factually reliable?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to talk in broad terms, Mr. Walker's mission was, on the one hand, an attempt to find a peaceful solution, to restore peace to Kosovo. And on the other hand, it was a detail, a cog in the wheel of that large operation that I talked about yesterday. For instance, on what basis did NATO constantly arrogate the right to concentrate its military forces, to assume functions that normally belonged to the United Nations, and to circumvent the legal bodies? And in this process of Kosovo and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, again. Mr. Nice, it's open to you to stop the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will if you want. It's just -- well, Your Honour, I'm always reluctant to interfere because interference has its negative side, but I will be more pro-active if the Chamber would like. It also sometimes gives the false impression that I'm troubled by the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no jury here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that -- I'm not grateful for that, I simply observe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, if you can't explain to me -- no. It's not for me. You raised yesterday that these reports are unreliable. I want to explore on what ground you're saying they're unreliable, because if you don't give a ground for their unreliability, I'm simply going to move on to another topic. Can you explain why, in factual terms, these reports are unreliable?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, those international commissions who were not under NATO's control provided different reports. Please note down I'm not going to comment. A Report of the OSCE, Kosovo, As Seen As Told. That was the name of the report. October 1998 - October 1999. That is also a report of the OSCE but outside of NATO control. And the conclusions you find there are completely different. There are some conclusions that coincide, there are others that don't. I also base my claim on the fact that the reports were made --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have the document. It's an exhibit in the case. It's being considered. Which conclusions are different?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions, in principle, are really different. I quote: "Prior to the NATO operation, Serb forces" -- and I underline "prior to the NATO operation," and you will not find this in Walker's report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said, "I quote." What are you quoting from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I'm quoting. It is the OSCE report just shown by Mr. Nice. It is an exhibit here, I understand. It is a report by independent experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... paragraph or chapter or page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I cannot give you the page because I just noted down certain excerpts from it in longhand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll allow you to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, there is a chapter about violence in Kosovo. May I quote, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll find it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll try to find it. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Prior to the NATO operation, the Serb army and organs of law enforcement acted harshly only in areas of concentration of the KLA. Punitive actions were targeted only against terrorists and separatist organisations openly supporting combat operations until they achieved freedom of their territory." If you compare this passage to its equivalent in Walker's report, you will see that the conclusions are very different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very good. We have the OSCE. In the break, Mr. Nice will try to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. General, can you tell us, was it from the first couple of pages of the book or did you read all of it or consider all of the book?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a chapter that speaks of the escalation of violence. That could be the title, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We're going to take a break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to caution you that I used up 215 minutes in my examination-in-chief. Mr. Nice is entitled to 60 per cent of my time, and he has already used 150 minutes, and you did not caution him in time. He has overstepped his time limit by a great deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On many occasions, Mr. Milosevic, you were allowed additional time in cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses. In the Chamber's view, the overtime is entirely appropriate and warranted on this occasion, but I take note of the point that you have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In event, it will be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I took the general encouragement to take the time allowed to be a global rather than a particular witness one, and a witness like this coming with the range of material without any warning was one who was going to take some time, but of course I'm absolutely anxious to be as short as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Milosevic, in any event, an adjustment will be made so there will be no loss of time to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid we can't find the reference in "As Seen, As Told." I would ask the usher just to lay on the overhead projector this passage highlighted in yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, General, you came to Court with one extract from "As Seen, As Told," the report There are two reports, by the way. I don't know if you knew that. This is the one we think you had in mind. You should know that this same report upon which you rely to show the unreliability of KVM reporting includes this in its executive summary or its opening paragraph: "The scale on which human rights violations recur is staggering. It has been estimated that over 90 per cent of the Kosovo Albanian population - over 1.45 million people - were displaced by the conflict by the 9 June 1999. The death toll as yet can only be guessed at, but the prevalence of confirmed reports and witness statements about individual and group killings in this report is indicative. The violence meted out to people as recounted vividly, particularly in the statements of refugees, was extreme and appalling." I don't want to read further. General, this is a report that you rely on to show the unreliability of the raw material before this Trial Chamber, but just help me, is this conclusion of the "As Seen, As Told" report something that you accept or not? Because it's part of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: What in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, where it's said that the scale of human rights violations is staggering and where it says that 1.45 million people were displaced, for example. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that insofar as the report deals with violations of human rights, primarily by terrorist organisations. As for the number of displaced persons, I cannot confirm it, but that the massive exodus of refugees began with the start of the NATO bombing is something that I support and confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that. Staying with the KVM, General Drewienkiewicz and Mr. Walker were not asked, no complaints to you about this, General, were not asked all the questions that were raised by your evidence yesterday. Please confirm that there was a Russian deputy, part of the KVM, who would have been present at every one of Ambassador Walker's morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you translate "Russian deputy"? Do you mean deputy to the parliament or a Russian representative?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. Representative.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Russian representative, yes, he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that any bias by Ambassador Walker or those reporting to him could have been detected by the Russian representative, documented, and then reflected in your evidence here?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me note that in October 19 -- excuse me, December 1998, our representative submitted a report to our Defence Minister Marshal Sergeyev and submitted another long report to me in which the representative noted precisely such facts; namely, that the reports by the Russian representative are received but not taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, have you --

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representative in question was Mr. Ivanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you brought that report with you?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that the question would arise. If I had known, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could have brought it, and I would probably have needed a whole plane to fill with documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. That specific report, you can get?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a verbal report, and I remember maps were laid out when he reported to the defence minister and briefed me. And that happened in Belgrade in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You said he submitted a report, which would lead one to believe that there was a written report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was a verbal report on the situation that had developed in the mission. The situation was that the input of the Russian and some other representatives of non-NATO countries were not being taken into account. That is what he reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when that report was submitted, that oral report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the marshal of Russia and simultaneously Defence Minister Sergeyev, there was myself and two of my officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, what was done about it in the light of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Marshal Sergeyev set the task of firmly promoting our interests and forwarding our reports to the headquarters so that they be taken into account. And upon return from Belgrade, he spoke about it at one of his meetings with NATO, and he also informed the foreign ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, General, if there is any substance in the complaint, you could have, or your marshal could have, complained to Vienna, could have complained to Ambassador Walker, could have required further detailed reporting to your representative who was at every one of Walker's daily meetings. Now, I cannot know one way or another what was said in an oral report, but what I suggest to you is that there's no real substance in the complaint that you're making; and indeed, just to complete it, had this been raised, the position of the Prosecution through witnesses would almost certainly have been that the Russians were very well used in the mission, were very well distributed, as were the Ukrainians, not least, of course, because the Ukrainians were able to communicate linquistically directly with the people on the ground. They were well used and well relied on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you putting that as a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm putting that as a proposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What could I do? Upon return to Russia, I could seek written confirmation from the observers who worked on the mission and forward these reports to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to move on from the reliability of the reports, because I don't think the witness can help us further. I would respectfully remind the Court of the exercise we went through with the blue book, and we've only had one ground-level witness, and that was the witness Keith. I'll just deal with that with this witness, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General Ivasov, I should ask for your comment on this. I don't know if you've seen the evidence or had it reported to you, but the only I think ground-level reporting officer, the man Keith, who was called by this accused as one of the accused's witnesses, produced a couple of his daily reports and found that everything in it, effectively, was faithfully reported in the compendious reporting document known as the blue book. Now, do you have any reason to doubt that the blue book is indeed an accurate - this is a compendious account - an accurate report of the events on the ground?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Keith, therefore, I cannot comment on the blue book. I based my opinion on the official documents that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the verbal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which official documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the same report by Mr. Walker, the OSCE documents, as well as the official reports sent in by the representatives of Russia within the mission who worked on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if there's any of this material that's going to be produced to us, but in the absence of it I'm just going to move on. May I help the Chamber in relation to one of the things or two of the things that the witness said yesterday. This calls for no answer by the witness, although he may wish to make a comment. It is accepted that there were present in the KVM at least some people who had been trained by or had experience with the American organisation MPRI, and I do not challenge that members of the KLA may have been trained by such people. The Rule 68 regime under which I now work has been recently changed by a change in the Rule, and the Chamber will understand the difficulties I sometimes face with producing in written form the material that I might wish to do, but I've made, I hope, adequate concessions to ensure that there is no unfairness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please clarify what you have in mind. I never stated that members of the Verification Mission had been recruited or used by that organisation. What I said was that in the territory of Albania, there were training camps where persons recruited by these organisations were observed. I never made that claim with respect to any members of the mission. Please take this into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honours, in light of the general complaints of or criticisms about Ambassador Walker, a short collection of documents, which I think I can deal with quite swiftly. They exist in both English translation and B/C/S, so that there can be a B/C/S version for the witness, although he may prefer to hear it through the English translation. They are reports from the federal ministry -- the federal foreign ministry office in Kosovo. And if they can be displayed on the overhead projector in the English version so that we can follow them very, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour? Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to inform you that I have my flight at 1600 hours today, leaving from Amsterdam.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like you to have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is 4.00. If you leave here at a quarter to two, you should get there before three. I think you're still on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first document, dated the 26th of November, 1998, described as a Drewienkiewicz conversation - that's General DZ, who was a witness here - and it just deals with the terminological problem of terrorism and the other party, and explains: "Drewienkiewicz agreed that the two parties could not be equated because one was a sovereign state and while the other party certainly was not, did they consider it -- nor did they consider it as such." This is a small point, but the terminology of terrorism or otherwise we've seen in the reports that we were looking at before, that Walker and others were prepared to describe the KLA as terrorists from time to time, and you would accept that, General, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely periodically. From time to time, they would call them terrorists. But the conduct of Mr. Walker was quite surprising, because he used to meet with the leaders of a terrorist organisation, and moreover, some representatives of the United States and other NATO Member States would meet with them in various European capitals. And there was no attempt to arrest them or interview them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause. As I've explained to you through the evidence, NATO was not allowed to meet terrorists, and the whole purpose of the KVM was that it should be able to meet -- one of the purposes of the KVM was that it should be able to negotiate with all sides, and that's what they did. Now, I thought you'd accepted that, but if you don't, I rather we can move on because of limited time.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the representatives of NATO countries would meet publicly and openly with leaders of a terrorist organisation. Moreover, they invited them to conferences and welcomed them warmly there. And they did not display such generosity with respect to the representatives of the official authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next document, please, has got an uncertain date but is probably the 16th of December. Its subject is Walker and Loncar, and at the bottom of the first page: "The subjects discussed included the latest incidents provoked by Albanian terrorists on the Yugoslav/Albanian border and an attack on a cafe in Pec where six Serbs were killed. What was characteristic for this conversation was that, for the first time, Walker described such incidents as terrorist acts, adding that a similar definition had been used by Ambassador Holbrooke." I think this confirms your account, I think, and we can move on, agreed?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the fact that this incident did take place. On that particular day I was in Belgrade, and yes, I agree with the fact that Mr. Walker did not ascribe clear legal responsibility for this incident to the terrorist organisation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document is the 28th of December, mistyped as '88 in the translation but it's 1998. So don't take any notice of the English translation. And the subject is a conversation between Drewienkiewicz and Loncar. Four lines down in the body of the report: "He said that he first wished to present the current assessments of the KVM on the political and security situation in Kosovo and Metohija, and the latest incidents which caused the negotiated cease-fire between the MUP and the so-called KLA to break down. In the way he presented the assessments and conclusions of the KVM, the focus of his assessment was that MUP and the Yugoslav army had acted in a legitimate way lately, but their use of force was disproportionate." We can go over the page, please, Usher. Two lines down on the next page: "He also underlined that, in his view, the KVM was doing its work well, even going beyond its tasks, since it not only endeavours to verify the situation but also to contact the KLA in order to exert pressure on the other side and convince them not to act foolishly, attempting to convince them to withdraw to the positions held in October of this year and that their provocations and 'strutting around' were inappropriate in the given situation." And then over the page, please, Usher, to the last page of -- effectively the last page of this report, seven lines down. "Wishing to emphasise the good intentions, refuted by our side,, of the KVM, he said that mission head Walker had given a positive statement with regard to the incidents on the Yugoslav-Albanian border. On that occasion, he clearly verified the entire event as the legitimate right of the Yugoslav side." So, now, this, you see, General, is a report by the Serb side on various things said by General Drewienkiewicz, and it is quite clear, is it not, from the material available that they were being evenhanded in what they were doing by way of reporting?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. In certain cases, especially when it had to do with attempted incursions across the border and also in some other instances, Mr. Walker did provide objective information. However, as for the claim that disproportionate force was used, there is no legal interpretation of that term. However, let me reiterate once again that all legislation and all orders dealing with the Supreme Command and commanding of armed forces limited the use of force and reiterated that those who violate regulations will be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the sixth, seventh time you've told us that, and I'm going to move on to the last document of this bundle. The 12th of January, 1999, again, a Serb-side report. Conversation with Aleksandar Nikolaev, chief, reconstruction, KVM. Can you help us, is Nikalaev a Russian?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. If you tell me more about the person, perhaps -- half of people in Russia has the name of Nikalaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But just look at what it says in paragraph, or listen, in your case, what it says in paragraph 2: "Nikalaev presented some details with regard to events in the KVM after the murder of the policemen and the abduction of Yugoslav army soldiers. Immediately upon receiving the news about the given incidents, General Drewienkiewicz informed Walker in Washington. Ambassador Walker asked General D. to hold off sending the report to Washington, 'warning' him that perhaps it was a matter of misinformation and so forth. "Nevertheless, General D. organised a meeting with Walker's other deputies. On the basis of a majority vote, it was decided to forward the report to Washington, as a result of which Walker was 'furious.' "In continuation, Nikalaev informed us about the assessment of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija drawn up by the KVM Department for Analytical Assessments on the 9th of January." Now, I'm not going to take any more time with that document, but it's clear, isn't it, that the workings of the KVM were transparent to a body like Russia in various ways. You had a representative at their morning meetings, full reports of any little disagreements were available, like this, which went to Yugoslavia, and it was a body doing a serious job in a responsible and transparent way; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment upon this particular case. However, I know that when Igor Ivanov, minister of foreign affairs of Russia, met with Mrs. Albright and other colleagues, he did put forward this issue, namely the issue on the objectivity of reporting on the events in Kosovo coming from all members of the mission. As for Mr. Holbrooke, that he was upset, this is an internal US affair, especially since Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Walker, as well as many other officials who served in European Commissions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- were representatives of the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can go on but I forecast the Chamber is interested in how much re-examination time the accused wants. If he wants any, then I can finish in perhaps 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, will you be re-examining; and if you will be, how long would you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll finish by 25 to, or 20 to, then. That would be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 25 to? I'd say half past.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is one important matter you raised yesterday, or potentially important matter, General, that the Chamber may want assistance with. You suggested that the KVM was actively pursuing the general plan to dismember Yugoslavia by identifying targets for bombing. That's what you said, effectively. What's your evidence for that, or do you in fact have none?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is evidence supporting that. However, so far, this evidence is classified, and it was contained in the report of those monitors, the report which I hope to provide to the Court upon my return to Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: General, I think you should reflect on what's happened so far. If you're going to refer to classified material, so far as I'm concerned, do so, but you must then -- we will then seek through the Court that you produce it. If you're not going to be able to produce it, I don't ask you to give any answers based on it. Now, are you going to be able to produce this classified material? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will refer to indirect information in areas where certain members of the mission worked. After the 24th of March, very direct and precise strikes were made, and the air reconnaissance in the area probably collected information. We have reasons to believe that they collected military intelligence information. There could not have been other reason for their presence. How many cases would be sufficient to substantiate my claim, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Armies such as NATO would have, by all sorts of contingency planning, advance knowledge of all fixed-location targets, would they not? They wouldn't be dependent on an ad hoc group of available staff produced for the KVM mission. They would have information way before that. As a military man, you must know that.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a military man, and I know that military men follow orders and legislation. Who authorised NATO to create armed groups and prepare air strikes? What organ, what body authorised this action? Was it Mr. Solana?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer the question. NATO would have had advance knowledge of target sites, and it would not require information from an ad hoc group like the KVM to do such work for it. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, when the Russian side supplied documents to Mr. Clark, documents on training camps for terrorists, routes used for them to supply weapons and other supplies, Mr. Clark claimed that NATO did not possess any such information and that its intelligence services was doing a poor job. So this is the only comment I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Next point. Next point.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Verification Mission probably complemented the work of NATO intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next point. The reports that we've heard, including "As Seen, As Told," the human rights report, and so on, and the evidence of somebody called Ball, an expert, all go to show or to suggest that expulsion following the start of the bombing campaign was as a result of action by Serb forces. I only want to know methodologically what is it that you rely on to suggest it? First of all, A, did you speak to the refugees yourself? That's a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I personally spoke through a Greek-Russian interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To how many?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the two of them who represented two families of Albanian Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What other evidence do you rely on to show that the bulk of the evidence coming to this court about the expulsions following Serb actions is wrong? What do you rely on?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also relied on the statements of the UN Commissioner for Refugees. I also relied on the UN documents indicating that there was an increase, dramatic increase in the number of refugees from the beginning of bombing. And yesterday I explained how this came about. People were looking for shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you from your intelligence have any explanation for how the Judges are in due course satisfied of this: Mass graves in Serbia Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. contained bodies of people killed in Kosovo, in particular at Batajnica, the special anti-terrorist unit based near Belgrade? Do you, from your intelligence, have any explanation for how that happened?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received regular information from our embassy, from the administration of military attache, and from other structures. We also received information from the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... explain, can you please help us, as a friendly nation with access to intelligence and information, how or why bodies of people killed in Kosovo were buried in an air force base -- near an air force base in Belgrade? Just yes or no, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with the burial of this -- these bodies, so I cannot comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't present at Rambouillet yourself?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present in Rambouillet. Russia was represented there by Boris Mayorsky, who, in the second round of negotiations, was not able to familiarise himself with the document presented by Mrs. Albright. And this is his own account of the event. And this document was immediately accepted by the Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reality, General Ivasov, is that you are extremely loyal to the Slav and Yugoslav cause as you perceive it; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you know what? I have a lot of friends in NATO. They continue to be my friends. And these are highly placed individuals. Mr. Solana decorated me with a medal for cooperation with NATO. But I have to say that I did not accept the medal. Mr. Robertson, General-Secretary of NATO, in May of 2001, awarded me with a special medal for my contribution to the cooperation with NATO. Yes, I am a patriot, I love my country, but let me reiterate, I was born in the Islamic republic within the Soviet Union, and I treat all ethnicities with respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you, for example, when it came to the agreement that ended the NATO bombing, were against the conciliatory approach taken by Chernomyrdin, your superior, and indeed you obstinately refused to approve of his agreement, requiring your own minister's approval of it before it could be effected; correct?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically declined, opposed the ultimatum issued to Yugoslavia. I categorically abided by the directive of the President Yeltsin, which was mandatory for all members of the delegation and which was violated by Mr. Chernomyrdin. I also opposed any secret dealings that took place between Mr. Talbot and Mr. Chernomyrdin. And let me give you an example. When Mr. Chernomyrdin and Mr. Atasari arrived in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can just ask you this, because I want you to look at a couple of clips and then I'm done, from a film. You were in fact the officer who took the Russian forces to Pristina airport, precipitating near conflict with NATO, and you had to withdraw them. Whether you did that on Yeltsin's instructions or on your own initiative not being clear, but you were the officer who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first of all, let us clarify something. What provision of the UN Charter or what paragraph of the UN Security Council Resolution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question? Can you answer the question whether you were the officer who took the Russian forces to Pristina airport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the officer who executed the order of President Yeltsin. The decision of President Yeltsin and the order of the minister of defence. I tried to comply with it to the best of my abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at some very short extracts from The Fall of Milosevic programme.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "First of all, when there were rallies, primarily outside the American embassy, I went there to see. I was dressed in mufti and I was really enthusiastic about our young people who evaluated this aggression as what it was, aggression."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Mr. Chernomyrdin had in his delegation a Russian general by the name of Ivasov. He said no to everything. Every conceivable proposition. NATO at the core, no; total withdrawals, no. You name it, the answer was no."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Moscow was clearly up to something. Clinton's Russian advisor was sent there to confront the Russian foreign minister."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Ivanov said that he regretted to inform us that there had indeed been an accidental deployment of Russian forces into Kosovo but that it was an accident and they would be out in a matter of hours."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "So contrite was the Russian foreign minister that he agreed to phone a statement to CNN."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "As early as he dared, the foreign minister woke his colleagues. "The foreign minister now learned that his president had been behind the whole operation. "They decided to raise the stakes and send reinforcements to Pristina airport."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "We were getting information reports that the --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you're now running into the re-examination time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All I was going to ask you is this, and it's my final question: Your reaction, we can't necessarily resolve if it was your initiative or President Yeltsin's order, but your reaction generally at the time of this agreement that brought to the end the bombing, and we'll hear more of this from other witnesses, shows sadly, General, that you are extremely committed, if not overcommitted, to what you see as the Yugoslav interest. Isn't that the reality?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... short answer to that, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, thank you for letting me see this footage. I was younger then. Second, I had in my hands the president's order, and I followed it. And I had no negative feelings towards the American delegation and even less towards the Finnish delegation. The three-star General Stugasin [phoen] and General Casey and I had a very friendly mutual relationship. There was no hostility. Yes, I did defend the interests of Yugoslavia as an independent sovereign country. I demanded and tried to achieve that the UN Charter and the international norms be observed. I did not pursue any other objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I am as dedicated to peace as any NATO General. The peace of Kosovo, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm going to exhibit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Please exhibit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are four other exhibits, but maybe we can deal with those after the re-examination so as not to cut into witness time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one brief topic, General Ivasov, in this cross-examination. Mr. Nice asked you questions related to the Verification Mission, although you spoke about it in detail yesterday. I will ask you, in my turn, a very, very brief question, and it is as follows: Did the Verification Mission headed by Walker -- was the Verification Mission used to achieve peace or to prepare an aggression against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to observe that many of the mission's members, especially those from Sweden, Finland, Ukraine, Russia, and others, and even some NATO member countries such as Greece, really did seek peace. However, there was a group of representatives who were solely involved in military issues, military tasks, namely the tasks of preparing the airstrikes, and some of them were representatives of the intelligence services of Western countries, and their primary job was an intelligence-gathering job. That intelligence job was done under the cover of the Verification Mission, preparing airstrikes and the ground operation that were to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did NATO cooperate with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That cooperation was on the political level. I quoted examples when leaders of terrorist organisations met with officials of NATO. The cooperation was also on the military level, because, particularly in autumn 1998, the terrorists' arsenal began to include state-of-the-art weapons manufactured in NATO member countries. Even Mr. Walker I can quote. On the 28th of September, immediately after meeting with you -- sorry, not Walker, Holbrooke. Holbrooke immediately went on to meet the leaders of the terrorist organisation, and so on and so forth. That can easily be considered as open cooperation with the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. terrorist organisation. Furthermore, there was no attempt whatsoever to arrest any of these murderers and terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Ivasov, in the interview you gave to the Nin magazine on the 5th of May, 1999, I will quote only one sentence from it. You said: "Even if President Milosevic and the Yugoslav government were to propose the most constructive and the most humane option for resolving the Kosovo crisis, which I repeat had been caused from outside, the NATO leadership headed by the US would, nevertheless, start with their operation." Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know where this is going. I know we are pressed for time, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have an objection to this and if the accused wants to run his case himself he's going to have to get used to the technical rules, and apart from the general limitation on relying on prior consistent statements, which we needn't debate now, simply to put a sentence that hasn't been explored in evidence to a witness in these circumstances doesn't to me to be likely to help the Chamber very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic. I take note of the point you make, Mr. Nice. Proceed. Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked General Ivasov was that his position. Does he still believe so today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he did answer yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am certain about this. That certainty was shared by the Russian political and military leadership. If Mr. Nice is still not satisfied, I can quote a sentence from the Washington Post and Houston Chronicle, and even Mr. Kissinger, who said in unison, "Did anyone ever imagine that Serbs could possibly accept this ultimatum --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've had your answer. I said, General, we've had your answer. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Evidence and proof of your claims to the effect that NATO had been preparing activities and aggression against Yugoslavia has been sought here. I want to ask, is it true that this claim of yours is also based on a great number of your face-to-face conversations with high officials of the NATO alliance? If you wish, you can enumerate by name the people from NATO with whom you discussed this issue, warning them that they should not go forward with this operation.

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke practically with all NATO leaders, with Mr. Solana, for instance, but I underline that Mr. Solana didn't take any decisions. Any American general took more decisions than him. With Mr. Robertson, with Colonel Naumann, and practically all defence ministers of NATO. Both the Russian official position and my personal position were the same; to avoid war. However, the machine was already in operation, and I can quote specific materials. 6th of May, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, General. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the dates when NATO gave official statements and announcements about the increasing readiness of their military forces and the upcoming operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I ask you already, do you have evidence that was sought here that NATO had been preparing the attack on Yugoslavia as early as mid-1998?

utterances.speaker: LEONID IVASOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Already in June, or even May, NATO had made official announcements, and our participation, our discussions in NATO-Russia discussions at defence minister level showed that NATO saw only two options, either the capitulation of Belgrade or the military operation. And when I was discussing within the NATO-Russia partnership, I tried to present arguments to Mr. Solana and others. I asked them, "Why are you delivering missiles?" And they said, "For the peacekeeping operation." And some of them said, "Whenever I see Mr. Ivasov raise his hand, I lose one hair off my head." So we did discuss these matters constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivasov. Safe trip home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, that -- General, that concludes your testimony. Thanks for coming to give it. You may now leave. And we are adjourned -- Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibits. We needn't detain the general from his flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, you may leave. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.
